PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Animals are living things. In this sub-strand you will find out the characteristics that show animals are alive, learn how to sort animals into vertebrates (animals with a backbone) and invertebrates (animals without a backbone), and learn how to care for animals and stay safe around them.

## Strand 1.0: Living Things and their Environment
Sub-strand 1.2: Animals
Suggested lessons: 12

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the characteristics of animals as living things
b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment
c) appreciate the need to care for animals

## What this sub-strand covers
• Characteristics of animals as living things
• Vertebrates and invertebrates

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are animals grouped as living things?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: The learner contributes to group decision making by participating actively as they discuss characteristics of animals as living things.
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner discovers new ways of solving problems of keeping records as they design and make a portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates.

## Values
• Responsibility: The learner takes care of the different materials they use as they search for information from print and non-print materials on main differences between vertebrates and invertebrates and share with peers.
• Respect: The learner appreciates divergent ideas from peers as they discuss their findings on characteristics of animals as living things.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Animal welfare: The learner takes care of animals during the learning activities.
• Safety and security: The learner observes safety when handling animals.

## Links to other learning areas
• Agriculture and Nutrition: The learner uses the information on characteristics of animals as living things in the study of livestock.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Science and Technology Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 1.0 Living Things and their Environment, Sub-strand 1.2 Animals

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Characteristics of animals as living things

LESSON 1: CHARACTERISTICS OF ANIMALS AS LIVING THINGS
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• State the characteristics that show animals are living things.
• Give examples of each characteristic from animals around you.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the characteristics of animals as living things

## Introduction
A hen pecks at maize, lays eggs, and some weeks later little chicks come out of the eggs. The chicks grow into hens and cocks. Everything the hen does tells us that it is alive.

## Notes
Animals are grouped as living things because they show all the characteristics of life. Animals:

- **Feed.** Animals cannot make their own food like green plants. They eat plants, other animals or both. A cow eats grass, a cat eats rats, and a hen eats grains and insects.
- **Grow.** A calf grows into a cow and a tadpole grows into a frog. Young animals get bigger as they feed.
- **Breathe.** Animals take in air (oxygen) and give out used air. People and cows breathe through the nose and lungs. Fish take in oxygen from water using gills.
- **Reproduce.** Animals make young ones of their own kind. Hens, ducks, snakes and most insects lay eggs. Cows, goats, dogs and people give birth to young ones.
- **Remove waste.** Animals get rid of waste from their bodies as urine and droppings (dung). We also give out used air and sweat.
- **Move.** Animals move from place to place to look for food, water and safety or to escape danger. Birds fly, fish swim, snakes crawl, frogs hop and goats walk.
- **Respond to changes in their environment.** A goat runs away when a dog barks. A millipede curls up when touched. Cows move into the shade when it is very hot.
- **Die.** All animals die at the end of their lives, or earlier because of disease, lack of food or injury.

### Plants and animals compared
Both plants and animals are living things. The main differences are that animals feed on ready-made food while green plants make their own, and most animals move from place to place while plants stay in one place.

When you observe animals, watch from a safe distance. Do not disturb nests, and never tease or hurt an animal.

## Key words
• characteristic — a feature that helps us describe or recognise something
• breathe — to take air in and give used air out
• gills — parts a fish uses to take in oxygen from water
• dung — the droppings of animals such as cows

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A millipede rolls into a ball when a learner touches it with a stick. Which characteristic of living things is this?

Working:
1. The millipede reacted to being touched.
2. Reacting to a change is responding.

Answer: Animals respond to changes in their environment.

### Example 2
Give one piece of evidence from a cow that shows it removes waste.

Working:
1. Waste leaves the body of an animal as urine and droppings.

Answer: The cow passes out dung and urine.

## Activity: Animal detectives
You will need: Notebook and pencil, A table with columns: Animal, What it did, Characteristic shown
1. Walk around the school compound and nearby area with your teacher.
2. Observe animals such as birds, insects, goats, chickens or cats from a safe distance.
3. Record what each animal did, for example 'bird flying' or 'chick feeding', and the characteristic it shows.
4. Look for other evidence such as droppings, eggs, nests and young animals.
5. Back in class, discuss your findings with your group. Wash your hands after the walk.

## Practice
1. List four characteristics of animals as living things.
2. How does a fish breathe?
3. Name two animals that lay eggs and two that give birth to young ones.
4. Why do animals move from place to place?

## Summary
• Animals feed, grow, breathe, reproduce, remove waste, move, respond to changes and die.
• Animals eat ready-made food; green plants make their own.
• Observe animals from a safe distance.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: feed, grow, breathe, reproduce, remove waste, move, respond to changes, die.
2. It takes in oxygen from water using its gills.
3. Lay eggs: hen, duck, snake, frog, most insects. Give birth: cow, goat, dog, rabbit, people.
4. To look for food, water, shelter or safety, and to escape danger.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Vertebrates: animals with a backbone

LESSON 2: VERTEBRATES: ANIMALS WITH A BACKBONE
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a vertebrate is.
• Name the groups of vertebrates and give examples.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
Run your fingers down the middle of your back. You can feel a line of small bones. This is your backbone. Many animals have one too, and scientists use it to sort animals into two big groups.

## Notes
The backbone is a long chain of small bones that runs along the middle of the back. It holds the body upright and protects the soft spinal cord inside it. Animals that have a backbone are called **vertebrates**.

Vertebrates have a skeleton of bones inside their bodies. Most vertebrates are bigger than invertebrates, and many have a clear head, body and tail or limbs.

### Groups of vertebrates
There are five main groups of vertebrates:

- **Mammals** – have hair or fur, give birth to young ones and feed them on milk. Examples: cow, goat, dog, cat, rabbit, monkey, elephant, human beings.
- **Birds** – have feathers, wings and a beak, and lay eggs with hard shells. Examples: hen, duck, dove, ostrich, eagle.
- **Reptiles** – have dry scaly skin and most lay eggs on land. Examples: lizard, snake, crocodile, tortoise.
- **Amphibians** – have smooth, moist skin and can live both in water and on land. They lay eggs in water. Examples: frog, toad.
- **Fish** – live in water, have fins and scales and breathe using gills. Examples: tilapia, Nile perch, catfish.

### How to tell if an animal is a vertebrate
- Feel or look for a backbone. In a fish you can see it as the long middle bone when you eat it.
- Remember the groups: if the animal is a mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian or fish, it is a vertebrate.

Not all animals in water are fish. A whale and a dolphin live in the sea but are mammals, because they breathe air and feed their young on milk. They still have a backbone, so they are vertebrates.

## Key words
• backbone — the chain of small bones along the middle of the back
• vertebrate — an animal that has a backbone
• mammal — a vertebrate with hair or fur that feeds its young on milk
• amphibian — a vertebrate with moist skin that can live in water and on land

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these vertebrates into their groups: goat, frog, dove, tilapia, lizard.

Working:
1. Goat has hair and feeds young on milk: mammal.
2. Frog has moist skin: amphibian.
3. Dove has feathers: bird.
4. Tilapia lives in water with fins: fish.
5. Lizard has dry scaly skin: reptile.

Answer: Goat – mammal, frog – amphibian, dove – bird, tilapia – fish, lizard – reptile.

## Activity: Find the backbone
You will need: The cleaned bones of a fish from a meal, or pictures of animal skeletons, Books or a digital device with pictures of animals
1. Feel your own backbone by running your fingers gently down your partner's back.
2. Look at the fish bones or skeleton pictures and point to the backbone.
3. Search in books or on a digital device for pictures of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
4. Make a table of the five groups and write two examples in each. Share it with your peers.

## Practice
1. What is a vertebrate?
2. Name the five groups of vertebrates.
3. Which group of vertebrates has feathers?
4. Is a snake a vertebrate? Give a reason.

## Summary
• Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.
• The five groups are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
• The backbone supports the body and protects the spinal cord.

### Answers to practice
1. An animal that has a backbone.
2. Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
3. Birds.
4. Yes. A snake has a backbone; it is a reptile.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Invertebrates and how they differ from vertebrates

LESSON 3: INVERTEBRATES AND HOW THEY DIFFER FROM VERTEBRATES
============================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what an invertebrate is and give examples.
• State the main differences between vertebrates and invertebrates.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
Lift a stone in a damp part of the school garden. You may find earthworms, millipedes, beetles or a snail. Press gently on an earthworm and you will not feel any bones. These animals have no backbone.

## Notes
Animals that do not have a backbone are called **invertebrates**. Most animals on Earth are invertebrates, but many of them are so small that we hardly notice them.

### Examples of invertebrates
- **Insects** – have six legs and a body in three parts. Examples: housefly, bee, butterfly, ant, grasshopper, mosquito, beetle.
- **Spiders and ticks** – have eight legs.
- **Millipedes and centipedes** – have long bodies with many legs.
- **Worms** – have soft, long bodies without legs. Examples: earthworm, tapeworm, roundworm.
- **Snails and slugs** – have soft bodies. A snail carries a hard shell on its back.
- **Water invertebrates** – such as crabs, jellyfish, octopus and starfish.

Some invertebrates, such as insects, crabs and millipedes, have a hard outer covering that protects their soft bodies. Others, such as earthworms and slugs, are soft all over.

### Main differences between vertebrates and invertebrates

- Backbone: vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not.
- Skeleton: vertebrates have a skeleton of bones inside the body; invertebrates have no bones, though some have a hard outer covering or shell.
- Size: most vertebrates are larger; most invertebrates are small.
- Examples: vertebrates – cow, hen, lizard, frog, fish; invertebrates – ant, spider, earthworm, snail, crab.

### Invertebrates in our lives
Many invertebrates are useful. Bees make honey and help flowers to form fruits. Earthworms make soil fertile and let air into it. Some invertebrates are harmful: mosquitoes spread malaria, houseflies spread germs to food, ticks attack livestock, and some worms live in our intestines and make us sick.

## Key words
• invertebrate — an animal that does not have a backbone
• insect — a small invertebrate with six legs and a body in three parts
• shell — a hard outer covering that protects a soft body

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these animals into vertebrates and invertebrates: rabbit, earthworm, crocodile, butterfly, snail, dove.

Working:
1. Rabbit, crocodile and dove have a backbone.
2. Earthworm, butterfly and snail have no backbone.

Answer: Vertebrates: rabbit, crocodile, dove. Invertebrates: earthworm, butterfly, snail.

### Example 2
A snail has a hard shell. Does that make it a vertebrate?

Working:
1. A vertebrate must have a backbone inside its body.
2. A shell is an outer covering, not a backbone.

Answer: No. A snail is an invertebrate because it has no backbone.

## Activity: Vertebrate or invertebrate hunt
You will need: Notebook, A clear jar with holes in the lid, A hand lens if available
1. Walk around the school compound and immediate environment in groups.
2. Look under stones, on leaves and near water for animals. Use a stick or leaf, not your bare hands, to move small animals.
3. Record each animal you see in two columns: Vertebrates and Invertebrates.
4. Do not pick up bees, wasps, spiders, scorpions, centipedes or snakes.
5. Put back any small animal exactly where you found it, then wash your hands.
6. Share your list with another group and compare.

## Practice
1. What is an invertebrate?
2. Give four examples of invertebrates.
3. State one difference between vertebrates and invertebrates.
4. Name one useful and one harmful invertebrate.

## Summary
• Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.
• Insects, spiders, worms, snails and millipedes are invertebrates.
• The main difference: vertebrates have a backbone, invertebrates do not.

### Answers to practice
1. An animal without a backbone.
2. Any four: ant, bee, butterfly, housefly, spider, earthworm, snail, millipede, crab.
3. Vertebrates have a backbone and a skeleton of bones inside; invertebrates have no backbone.
4. Useful: bee or earthworm. Harmful: mosquito, housefly, tick or tapeworm.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Caring for animals and making a portfolio

LESSON 4: CARING FOR ANIMALS AND MAKING A PORTFOLIO
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Describe ways of caring for animals.
• Make a portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the need to care for animals; b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
A goat tied in the sun all day without water, or a dog that is beaten, suffers just as a person would. Animals feel pain, hunger and thirst, so they depend on people to treat them well.

## Notes
### Why we care for animals
Animals give us food such as milk, eggs, meat and honey. They give us wool and leather, help farmers to plough and carry loads, and keep our homes safe. Cats catch rats, and bees help crops to form fruits. Wild animals attract visitors to Kenya's parks. Animals are living things that can feel pain, so they deserve kindness.

### How to care for animals
- Give them enough clean water and the right food every day.
- Give them a clean, dry shelter that protects them from rain, cold and too much sun.
- Keep their shelter clean by removing dung.
- Take sick animals to a veterinary officer.
- Do not beat, tease, overload or throw stones at animals.
- Do not destroy the nests or homes of birds and other small animals.
- Handle small animals gently and return them to where you found them.

### Staying safe
- Do not touch animals that you do not know, such as stray dogs.
- Keep away from snakes, scorpions, bees and wasps, and tell an adult if you see one.
- Wash your hands with soap and water after touching animals or their droppings.

### Making a portfolio
A portfolio is a collection of your work kept in a file or folder. For this project you will make a portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates:

- Use a file or make a folder from old manila paper or a cereal box.
- Make one section for vertebrates and one for invertebrates.
- Add drawings or pictures cut from old magazines and newspapers.
- Under each picture write the animal's name and one fact, for example: 'Frog – amphibian, has a backbone, lives in water and on land.'
- Keep adding animals you observe during the term.

## Key words
• animal welfare — making sure animals are well fed, healthy and not treated cruelly
• veterinary officer — a person trained to treat sick animals
• portfolio — a collection of a learner's work kept in a file or folder

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A boy sees his neighbour's donkey carrying a very heavy load and being beaten. Is this proper care? What should be done?

Working:
1. Overloading and beating cause the donkey pain.
2. Proper care means a fair load, rest, food and water, and no beating.

Answer: No. The donkey should carry a load it can manage, be given rest, water and food, and never be beaten.

## Activity: Project: portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates
You will need: Old manila paper, a cereal box or a file, Old magazines and newspapers, Glue, scissors, crayons and pencils
1. In your group, decide on a cover design and the title for your portfolio.
2. Divide the portfolio into two sections: Vertebrates and Invertebrates.
3. Draw or cut out pictures of at least five animals for each section.
4. Write the name of each animal and one fact about it.
5. Share the tasks so that every member contributes, then present your portfolio to the class.

## Practice
1. Give three ways of caring for a pet dog.
2. Why should you wash your hands after handling animals?
3. What is a portfolio?

## Summary
• Animals give us food, materials, help with work and company.
• Care for animals with food, water, shelter, cleanliness and treatment when sick.
• Keep a portfolio to record the vertebrates and invertebrates you study.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: give it food and clean water, give it shelter, keep it clean, take it to a vet when sick, do not beat it.
2. To remove germs from the animal or its droppings that could make you sick.
3. A collection of your work kept in a file or folder.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: How animals feed, grow and breathe

LESSON 5: HOW ANIMALS FEED, GROW AND BREATHE
============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how feeding, growth and breathing show that animals are living things.
• Give safe examples of each characteristic from animals around you.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the characteristics of animals as living things

## Introduction
A calf drinks milk, then later eats grass, and month by month it becomes a larger cow. Watch its sides while it rests and you will see them move as it breathes.

## Notes
Three characteristics show clearly that animals are living things: they feed, they grow and they breathe. You can observe all three on animals around school and at home, if you watch from a safe distance and do not tease them.

### Feeding
Green plants make their own food. Animals cannot. Every animal must eat.

- Some animals eat plants. Cows, goats, sheep and rabbits eat grass and leaves.
- Some animals eat other animals. A cat hunts rats, a frog eats insects, and an eagle eats small animals.
- Some animals eat both. A hen eats grains and also insects. People eat foods from plants and from animals.

The food becomes the materials an animal uses to grow and to move. A young animal that does not get enough food grows poorly. Do not try to feed wild animals, and do not take food from a farm animal without permission. Observe what they already eat.

### Growth
Growth means the animal gets bigger and its body changes.

- A calf grows into a cow or a bull. Horns may appear as it gets older.
- A chick grows adult feathers and becomes a hen or a cock.
- A tadpole hatches from an egg in water. It has a tail and gills. Later it grows legs, the tail shortens, and it becomes a frog that can live on land.

You can record growth without touching the animal. Compare a young goat with an adult goat: size, horns and coat. If your family keeps chickens, note how a chick looks this month and how it looks next month.

### Breathing
Breathing takes oxygen into the body and pushes used air out.

- Cows, goats, birds, people and adult frogs breathe with lungs. Watch a resting cow: the sides of the body move in and out.
- Fish breathe with gills. Water passes over the gills and oxygen is taken from the water. The covers on the sides of the head open and close. A fish cannot breathe air the way a cow does.
- A tadpole breathes with gills while it lives in water. The adult frog breathes with lungs.

Never hold a fish out of water or cover an animal's nose to test this. Watching is enough evidence that animals breathe.

## Key words
• oxygen — the part of air, and of water, that animals need when they breathe
• lungs — the body parts used for breathing by mammals, birds, reptiles and adult frogs
• tadpole — the young stage of a frog, living in water and breathing with gills

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner lists what a hen does in one morning: it pecks grains, its chest moves as it rests, and the chicks beside it are bigger than they were last month. Which three characteristics are these?

Working:
1. Pecking grains is feeding.
2. The moving chest is breathing.
3. Chicks becoming bigger is growth.

Answer: Feeding, breathing and growth.

### Example 2
Why is it wrong to lift a fish out of a basin for several minutes to "see if it breathes"?

Working:
1. A fish takes oxygen from water using gills.
2. Out of water it cannot breathe properly and can die.

Answer: A fish breathes in water with its gills. Lifting it out can harm or kill it. Watch the gill covers while it is in the water.

## Activity: Record feeding, growth and breathing
You will need: Notebook, A table with columns: Animal, Feeding, Growth, Breathing
1. With your teacher, observe animals around the school compound from a safe distance.
2. For each animal, write what it eats or how it feeds, any sign that it grows, and how it breathes.
3. Use pictures in a book or on a digital device for animals you cannot see, such as a tadpole or a fish.
4. Discuss the table with your group. Add evidence another group found.
5. Do not touch or feed the animals. Wash your hands after the walk.

## Practice
1. Why must animals feed, while green plants do not have to eat?
2. Give one sign of growth in a frog's life.
3. How can you tell that a resting cow is breathing?
4. Name the parts a fish uses to breathe.

## Summary
• Animals feed on plants, other animals, or both.
• Young animals grow and their bodies change as they become adults.
• Mammals, birds and adult frogs use lungs. Fish and tadpoles use gills.

### Answers to practice
1. Animals cannot make their own food. Green plants make food in their leaves.
2. A tadpole grows legs and becomes a frog (or a calf becomes a cow, or a chick grows adult feathers).
3. The sides of its body move in and out.
4. Gills.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Mammals and birds

LESSON 6: MAMMALS AND BIRDS
===========================

## What you will learn
• Describe the features of mammals and of birds.
• Use those features to sort animals into the two groups.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
A goat has hair and the mother feeds her kid on milk. A dove has feathers and sits on hard-shelled eggs. Both animals have a backbone, but they belong to different groups.

## Notes
Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. They are sorted into five groups. This lesson looks closely at two of those groups: mammals and birds. Both groups have a skeleton of bones inside the body.

### Mammals
Mammals:

- Have a backbone.
- Have hair or fur. A cat's coat is fur. People have hair. Even an elephant has some hairs on its body.
- Feed their young on milk from the mother.
- Include familiar animals that give birth to live young. A cow gives birth to a calf, a goat to a kid, and a dog to puppies.

Mammals you may see near home include cows, goats, sheep, donkeys, dogs, cats and rabbits. Wild mammals include lions, zebras, elephants and monkeys.

Some mammals live in water. A whale and a dolphin have no gills and no scales like a fish. They come to the surface to breathe air, they have a backbone, and the mother feeds the young on milk. They are mammals, not fish.

### Birds
Birds:

- Have a backbone.
- Have feathers, a beak and two wings.
- Have no teeth. The beak matches the food. A hen's beak pecks seeds. A duck's beak is broad for feeding in water.
- Lay eggs with hard shells. A parent keeps the eggs warm until the chicks hatch.

Most birds fly. Feathers and wings make flight possible. An ostrich has feathers and wings but does not fly. It runs on strong legs. A hen flaps for a short distance but does not fly like a dove. Both are still birds because of their feathers and beaks.

### Sorting rule
Look at the body covering and at how the young are fed. Hair or fur, and a baby fed on milk, means a mammal. Feathers and a beak mean a bird. If you are building a portfolio, put these animals on the vertebrates pages and write the group name under each picture.

## Key words
• fur — the hairy coat of many mammals
• beak — the hard mouth of a bird, used for feeding
• milk — the food a mammal mother produces for her young

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these animals into mammals and birds: cat, ostrich, dolphin, dove, goat.

Working:
1. Cat, dolphin and goat have a backbone, and the young are fed on milk. They are mammals.
2. Ostrich and dove have feathers and beaks. They are birds.

Answer: Mammals: cat, dolphin, goat. Birds: ostrich, dove.

### Example 2
An ostrich cannot fly. A classmate says it is therefore not a bird. What features show that it is a bird?

Working:
1. Birds are identified by feathers, a beak, wings and hard-shelled eggs.
2. Flight is common but not the feature that decides the group.

Answer: An ostrich has feathers, wings and a beak, and it lays hard-shelled eggs. Those features make it a bird.

## Activity: Picture sort: mammal or bird
You will need: Pictures from old magazines, newspapers or a digital search the teacher guides, Two large sheets labelled Mammals and Birds, Glue or a notebook for drawing
1. Collect or draw at least four mammals and four birds. Search print or digital materials for any animal you are not sure about.
2. Place each picture on the correct sheet and write one feature that proves your choice, such as "fur" or "feathers".
3. Include one tricky animal, such as a dolphin or an ostrich, and explain it to the class.
4. Add the best pictures to the vertebrates section of your portfolio.
5. Take care of the books and devices you use, and return them neatly.

## Practice
1. State two features of a mammal.
2. Why is a dolphin a mammal and not a fish?
3. State two features of a bird.
4. A hen does not fly long distances. Is it still a bird? Why?

## Summary
• Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.
• Birds have feathers and a beak, and they lay hard-shelled eggs.
• Whales and dolphins are mammals. An ostrich is a bird even though it does not fly.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: has a backbone, has hair or fur, feeds young on milk, gives birth to live young (for familiar mammals).
2. It breathes air, has a backbone, and feeds its young on milk. It does not have gills.
3. Any two: feathers, beak, wings, hard-shelled eggs, a backbone.
4. Yes. It has feathers, wings and a beak, and it lays hard-shelled eggs.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Reptiles, amphibians and fish

LESSON 7: REPTILES, AMPHIBIANS AND FISH
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the features of reptiles, amphibians and fish.
• Sort vertebrates into these three groups using skin, breathing and where they live.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
A lizard basks on a warm wall, a frog sits at the edge of a puddle, and a tilapia stays under the water. All three have a backbone, yet each belongs to a different group.

## Notes
The other three groups of vertebrates are reptiles, amphibians and fish. Each group has a backbone. The skin, the place they live and the way they breathe help you tell them apart.

### Reptiles
Reptiles have dry skin covered with scales. Most of them lay eggs on land. The shell of the egg is leathery, not hard like a bird's egg.

- A lizard has four legs and a tail, and it often rests in the sun.
- A snake has no legs, but it has a long backbone and scaly skin, so it is a reptile.
- A crocodile lives near water, but it has scaly skin and breathes with lungs.
- A tortoise has a shell on the outside and a backbone inside. That backbone makes it a vertebrate. A snail also has a shell, but a snail has no backbone, so a snail is an invertebrate.

Do not pick up snakes or go near crocodiles. Observe them only from far away, or use pictures in a book.

### Amphibians
Amphibians have soft, moist skin and no scales. They use both water and land. Frogs and toads lay eggs in water. The eggs have no hard shell. A frog's egg hatches into a tadpole, which breathes with gills. The tadpole grows legs and becomes an adult frog that breathes with lungs and can hop on land. A toad is also an amphibian. Its skin is bumpier than a frog's, but it still needs moisture and still begins life in water.

### Fish
Fish live in water. They have fins, and most have scales. They breathe with gills, not lungs. Tilapia and catfish are fish. Most fish lay eggs in water. When a fish is prepared as food you can see the backbone running along the body. That backbone is the evidence that a fish is a vertebrate.

### A quick test
Ask three questions. Is the skin dry and scaly? Think of a reptile. Is the skin moist, and does the animal use both water and land? Think of an amphibian. Does it have fins and gills and live in water? Think of a fish. Then remember that all three groups have a backbone, so all of them are vertebrates.

## Key words
• scales — the small hard plates that cover the skin of reptiles and most fish
• reptile — a vertebrate with dry scaly skin, such as a lizard, snake, crocodile or tortoise
• fins — the flat parts a fish uses for swimming

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these vertebrates: toad, catfish, snake, tortoise.

Working:
1. A toad has moist skin and uses water and land: amphibian.
2. A catfish has fins and gills: fish.
3. A snake and a tortoise have dry scaly skin: reptiles.

Answer: Toad: amphibian. Catfish: fish. Snake and tortoise: reptiles.

### Example 2
A tortoise and a snail both have shells. Which one is a vertebrate, and why?

Working:
1. A vertebrate must have a backbone inside the body.
2. A tortoise has a backbone. A snail does not.

Answer: The tortoise is a vertebrate because it has a backbone. The snail is an invertebrate.

## Activity: Three-group chart
You will need: Manila paper or an exercise book, Pictures or a textbook, Coloured pencils
1. Divide a page into three columns: Reptiles, Amphibians, Fish.
2. Search print or digital materials and write two examples in each column, plus one feature of that group.
3. Add a note on how each group breathes: lungs or gills.
4. Share the chart with another group and correct any animal placed in the wrong column.
5. Do not bring live snakes, frogs from protected places, or fish out of water into class. Use pictures.

## Practice
1. Why is a snake a reptile even though it has no legs?
2. Where do frogs lay their eggs, and what hatches from them?
3. State two features of a fish.
4. Name the five groups of vertebrates.

## Summary
• Reptiles have dry scaly skin. Most lay eggs on land.
• Amphibians have moist skin and begin life in water, like a frog and its tadpole.
• Fish have fins and gills and live in water. All three groups are vertebrates.

### Answers to practice
1. It has a backbone and dry scaly skin, and it is not a fish, amphibian, bird or mammal.
2. In water. A tadpole hatches from the egg.
3. Any two: lives in water, has fins, has scales, breathes with gills, has a backbone.
4. Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: Insects and other invertebrates

LESSON 8: INSECTS AND OTHER INVERTEBRATES
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Identify an insect using its body parts and six legs.
• Give examples of useful and harmful invertebrates and handle them safely.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment; c) appreciate the need to care for animals

## Introduction
Count the legs on a grasshopper and you will find six. Count the legs on a spider and you will find eight. That count, together with the missing backbone, tells you how to sort these small animals.

## Notes
Most of the animals on Earth have no backbone. They are invertebrates. Many are small, and you can find them in the school compound if you look carefully under leaves, stones and near flowers. Look without hurting them.

### Insects
An insect is an invertebrate with:

- A body in three parts, called the head, the thorax and the abdomen.
- Six legs, all joined to the thorax.
- A pair of feelers on the head.
- Often wings on the adult. Butterflies, bees and houseflies have wings. The ants you see walking on a path usually have no wings, but they still have six legs and three body parts, so they are insects.

Count the legs before you decide. A spider has eight legs, so a spider is not an insect. A millipede has many more than six legs. An earthworm has no legs at all. All of these are still invertebrates, because none of them has a backbone.

### Other invertebrates nearby
Earthworms live in moist soil. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil, and their waste adds useful matter to the soil. Snails have a soft body and a shell. The shell is not a backbone. Millipedes curl up when touched. That response shows they are living things, and the lack of a backbone shows they are invertebrates.

### Useful and harmful invertebrates
Some invertebrates help people. Bees visit flowers, help fruits to form, and make honey. Earthworms improve soil for crops. Some invertebrates cause harm. Mosquitoes can spread malaria. Houseflies land on dirt and then on uncovered food, carrying germs. Ticks bite livestock and can spread disease to the animals. Some worms can live inside the human intestine and make a person ill. That is one reason people take deworming medicine when a health worker or a parent gives it.

### Safety and care
Use a stick or a leaf to turn a stone, not your bare hands. Do not touch bees, wasps, spiders, scorpions or centipedes. Do not destroy nests or pull wings off insects. If you put a small animal in a jar to look at it, make holes in the lid, look for a short time, and put the animal back where you found it. Wash your hands afterwards. Caring for animals includes these small ones. Add your drawings to the invertebrates section of your portfolio.

## Key words
• thorax — the middle body part of an insect, where the legs and wings are joined
• abdomen — the rear body part of an insect
• feelers — the pair of long parts on an insect's head, used for sensing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner finds a small animal with eight legs and no wings. A second animal has six legs, three body parts and wings. Which one is an insect?

Working:
1. Insects have six legs and three body parts.
2. Eight legs means the first animal is not an insect. It is likely a spider.

Answer: The animal with six legs, three body parts and wings is an insect. The eight-legged animal is not.

### Example 2
Name one helpful invertebrate and one harmful invertebrate, and state what each does.

Working:
1. Bees help flowers form fruits and make honey. Earthworms improve soil.
2. Mosquitoes can spread malaria. Houseflies carry germs to food. Ticks harm livestock.

Answer: Helpful: a bee, which helps fruits to form, or an earthworm, which improves soil. Harmful: a mosquito, a housefly or a tick.

## Activity: Invertebrate hunt with a safety rule
You will need: Notebook, A hand lens if available, A clear jar with holes in the lid, Portfolio folder
1. Walk in the school compound with your teacher and look for invertebrates on plants, in soil and near flowers.
2. Record each animal, the number of legs if you can see them, and whether you think it is an insect.
3. Do not touch bees, wasps, spiders, scorpions, centipedes or snakes. Put any animal you jar back in the same place.
4. Mark one helpful and one harmful invertebrate on your list and explain each to your group.
5. Wash your hands, then file the list in your portfolio under Invertebrates.

## Practice
1. State two features that show an animal is an insect.
2. Why is a spider not an insect?
3. Give one way earthworms help plants.
4. What should you do after observing small animals?

## Summary
• Insects have six legs and three body parts, and they have no backbone.
• Spiders, worms, snails and millipedes are invertebrates but not all of them are insects.
• Observe small animals gently, learn which ones help or harm, and wash your hands.

### Answers to practice
1. Six legs and a body in three parts (also feelers, and often wings). It has no backbone.
2. A spider has eight legs. An insect has six.
3. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil, and their waste makes the soil richer.
4. Return them to the place you found them and wash your hands.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Animals are living things. In this sub-strand you will find out the characteristics that show animals are alive, learn how to sort animals into vertebrates (animals with a backbone) and invertebrates (animals without a backbone), and learn how to care for animals and stay safe around them.

## Strand 1.0: Living Things and their Environment
Sub-strand 1.2: Animals
Suggested lessons: 12

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the characteristics of animals as living things
b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment
c) appreciate the need to care for animals

## What this sub-strand covers
• Characteristics of animals as living things
• Vertebrates and invertebrates

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are animals grouped as living things?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: The learner contributes to group decision making by participating actively as they discuss characteristics of animals as living things.
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner discovers new ways of solving problems of keeping records as they design and make a portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates.

## Values
• Responsibility: The learner takes care of the different materials they use as they search for information from print and non-print materials on main differences between vertebrates and invertebrates and share with peers.
• Respect: The learner appreciates divergent ideas from peers as they discuss their findings on characteristics of animals as living things.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Animal welfare: The learner takes care of animals during the learning activities.
• Safety and security: The learner observes safety when handling animals.

## Links to other learning areas
• Agriculture and Nutrition: The learner uses the information on characteristics of animals as living things in the study of livestock.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Science and Technology Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 1.0 Living Things and their Environment, Sub-strand 1.2 Animals

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Characteristics of animals as living things
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: CHARACTERISTICS OF ANIMALS AS LIVING THINGS
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• State the characteristics that show animals are living things.
• Give examples of each characteristic from animals around you.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the characteristics of animals as living things

## Introduction
A hen pecks at maize, lays eggs, and some weeks later little chicks come out of the eggs. The chicks grow into hens and cocks. Everything the hen does tells us that it is alive.

## Notes
Animals are grouped as living things because they show all the characteristics of life. Animals:

- **Feed.** Animals cannot make their own food like green plants. They eat plants, other animals or both. A cow eats grass, a cat eats rats, and a hen eats grains and insects.
- **Grow.** A calf grows into a cow and a tadpole grows into a frog. Young animals get bigger as they feed.
- **Breathe.** Animals take in air (oxygen) and give out used air. People and cows breathe through the nose and lungs. Fish take in oxygen from water using gills.
- **Reproduce.** Animals make young ones of their own kind. Hens, ducks, snakes and most insects lay eggs. Cows, goats, dogs and people give birth to young ones.
- **Remove waste.** Animals get rid of waste from their bodies as urine and droppings (dung). We also give out used air and sweat.
- **Move.** Animals move from place to place to look for food, water and safety or to escape danger. Birds fly, fish swim, snakes crawl, frogs hop and goats walk.
- **Respond to changes in their environment.** A goat runs away when a dog barks. A millipede curls up when touched. Cows move into the shade when it is very hot.
- **Die.** All animals die at the end of their lives, or earlier because of disease, lack of food or injury.

### Plants and animals compared
Both plants and animals are living things. The main differences are that animals feed on ready-made food while green plants make their own, and most animals move from place to place while plants stay in one place.

When you observe animals, watch from a safe distance. Do not disturb nests, and never tease or hurt an animal.

## Key words
• characteristic — a feature that helps us describe or recognise something
• breathe — to take air in and give used air out
• gills — parts a fish uses to take in oxygen from water
• dung — the droppings of animals such as cows

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A millipede rolls into a ball when a learner touches it with a stick. Which characteristic of living things is this?

Working:
1. The millipede reacted to being touched.
2. Reacting to a change is responding.

Answer: Animals respond to changes in their environment.

### Example 2
Give one piece of evidence from a cow that shows it removes waste.

Working:
1. Waste leaves the body of an animal as urine and droppings.

Answer: The cow passes out dung and urine.

## Activity: Animal detectives
You will need: Notebook and pencil, A table with columns: Animal, What it did, Characteristic shown
1. Walk around the school compound and nearby area with your teacher.
2. Observe animals such as birds, insects, goats, chickens or cats from a safe distance.
3. Record what each animal did, for example 'bird flying' or 'chick feeding', and the characteristic it shows.
4. Look for other evidence such as droppings, eggs, nests and young animals.
5. Back in class, discuss your findings with your group. Wash your hands after the walk.

## Practice
1. List four characteristics of animals as living things.
2. How does a fish breathe?
3. Name two animals that lay eggs and two that give birth to young ones.
4. Why do animals move from place to place?

## Summary
• Animals feed, grow, breathe, reproduce, remove waste, move, respond to changes and die.
• Animals eat ready-made food; green plants make their own.
• Observe animals from a safe distance.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: feed, grow, breathe, reproduce, remove waste, move, respond to changes, die.
2. It takes in oxygen from water using its gills.
3. Lay eggs: hen, duck, snake, frog, most insects. Give birth: cow, goat, dog, rabbit, people.
4. To look for food, water, shelter or safety, and to escape danger.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Vertebrates: animals with a backbone
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: VERTEBRATES: ANIMALS WITH A BACKBONE
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a vertebrate is.
• Name the groups of vertebrates and give examples.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
Run your fingers down the middle of your back. You can feel a line of small bones. This is your backbone. Many animals have one too, and scientists use it to sort animals into two big groups.

## Notes
The backbone is a long chain of small bones that runs along the middle of the back. It holds the body upright and protects the soft spinal cord inside it. Animals that have a backbone are called **vertebrates**.

Vertebrates have a skeleton of bones inside their bodies. Most vertebrates are bigger than invertebrates, and many have a clear head, body and tail or limbs.

### Groups of vertebrates
There are five main groups of vertebrates:

- **Mammals** – have hair or fur, give birth to young ones and feed them on milk. Examples: cow, goat, dog, cat, rabbit, monkey, elephant, human beings.
- **Birds** – have feathers, wings and a beak, and lay eggs with hard shells. Examples: hen, duck, dove, ostrich, eagle.
- **Reptiles** – have dry scaly skin and most lay eggs on land. Examples: lizard, snake, crocodile, tortoise.
- **Amphibians** – have smooth, moist skin and can live both in water and on land. They lay eggs in water. Examples: frog, toad.
- **Fish** – live in water, have fins and scales and breathe using gills. Examples: tilapia, Nile perch, catfish.

### How to tell if an animal is a vertebrate
- Feel or look for a backbone. In a fish you can see it as the long middle bone when you eat it.
- Remember the groups: if the animal is a mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian or fish, it is a vertebrate.

Not all animals in water are fish. A whale and a dolphin live in the sea but are mammals, because they breathe air and feed their young on milk. They still have a backbone, so they are vertebrates.

## Key words
• backbone — the chain of small bones along the middle of the back
• vertebrate — an animal that has a backbone
• mammal — a vertebrate with hair or fur that feeds its young on milk
• amphibian — a vertebrate with moist skin that can live in water and on land

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these vertebrates into their groups: goat, frog, dove, tilapia, lizard.

Working:
1. Goat has hair and feeds young on milk: mammal.
2. Frog has moist skin: amphibian.
3. Dove has feathers: bird.
4. Tilapia lives in water with fins: fish.
5. Lizard has dry scaly skin: reptile.

Answer: Goat – mammal, frog – amphibian, dove – bird, tilapia – fish, lizard – reptile.

## Activity: Find the backbone
You will need: The cleaned bones of a fish from a meal, or pictures of animal skeletons, Books or a digital device with pictures of animals
1. Feel your own backbone by running your fingers gently down your partner's back.
2. Look at the fish bones or skeleton pictures and point to the backbone.
3. Search in books or on a digital device for pictures of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
4. Make a table of the five groups and write two examples in each. Share it with your peers.

## Practice
1. What is a vertebrate?
2. Name the five groups of vertebrates.
3. Which group of vertebrates has feathers?
4. Is a snake a vertebrate? Give a reason.

## Summary
• Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.
• The five groups are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
• The backbone supports the body and protects the spinal cord.

### Answers to practice
1. An animal that has a backbone.
2. Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
3. Birds.
4. Yes. A snake has a backbone; it is a reptile.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Invertebrates and how they differ from vertebrates
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: INVERTEBRATES AND HOW THEY DIFFER FROM VERTEBRATES
============================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what an invertebrate is and give examples.
• State the main differences between vertebrates and invertebrates.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
Lift a stone in a damp part of the school garden. You may find earthworms, millipedes, beetles or a snail. Press gently on an earthworm and you will not feel any bones. These animals have no backbone.

## Notes
Animals that do not have a backbone are called **invertebrates**. Most animals on Earth are invertebrates, but many of them are so small that we hardly notice them.

### Examples of invertebrates
- **Insects** – have six legs and a body in three parts. Examples: housefly, bee, butterfly, ant, grasshopper, mosquito, beetle.
- **Spiders and ticks** – have eight legs.
- **Millipedes and centipedes** – have long bodies with many legs.
- **Worms** – have soft, long bodies without legs. Examples: earthworm, tapeworm, roundworm.
- **Snails and slugs** – have soft bodies. A snail carries a hard shell on its back.
- **Water invertebrates** – such as crabs, jellyfish, octopus and starfish.

Some invertebrates, such as insects, crabs and millipedes, have a hard outer covering that protects their soft bodies. Others, such as earthworms and slugs, are soft all over.

### Main differences between vertebrates and invertebrates

- Backbone: vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not.
- Skeleton: vertebrates have a skeleton of bones inside the body; invertebrates have no bones, though some have a hard outer covering or shell.
- Size: most vertebrates are larger; most invertebrates are small.
- Examples: vertebrates – cow, hen, lizard, frog, fish; invertebrates – ant, spider, earthworm, snail, crab.

### Invertebrates in our lives
Many invertebrates are useful. Bees make honey and help flowers to form fruits. Earthworms make soil fertile and let air into it. Some invertebrates are harmful: mosquitoes spread malaria, houseflies spread germs to food, ticks attack livestock, and some worms live in our intestines and make us sick.

## Key words
• invertebrate — an animal that does not have a backbone
• insect — a small invertebrate with six legs and a body in three parts
• shell — a hard outer covering that protects a soft body

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these animals into vertebrates and invertebrates: rabbit, earthworm, crocodile, butterfly, snail, dove.

Working:
1. Rabbit, crocodile and dove have a backbone.
2. Earthworm, butterfly and snail have no backbone.

Answer: Vertebrates: rabbit, crocodile, dove. Invertebrates: earthworm, butterfly, snail.

### Example 2
A snail has a hard shell. Does that make it a vertebrate?

Working:
1. A vertebrate must have a backbone inside its body.
2. A shell is an outer covering, not a backbone.

Answer: No. A snail is an invertebrate because it has no backbone.

## Activity: Vertebrate or invertebrate hunt
You will need: Notebook, A clear jar with holes in the lid, A hand lens if available
1. Walk around the school compound and immediate environment in groups.
2. Look under stones, on leaves and near water for animals. Use a stick or leaf, not your bare hands, to move small animals.
3. Record each animal you see in two columns: Vertebrates and Invertebrates.
4. Do not pick up bees, wasps, spiders, scorpions, centipedes or snakes.
5. Put back any small animal exactly where you found it, then wash your hands.
6. Share your list with another group and compare.

## Practice
1. What is an invertebrate?
2. Give four examples of invertebrates.
3. State one difference between vertebrates and invertebrates.
4. Name one useful and one harmful invertebrate.

## Summary
• Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.
• Insects, spiders, worms, snails and millipedes are invertebrates.
• The main difference: vertebrates have a backbone, invertebrates do not.

### Answers to practice
1. An animal without a backbone.
2. Any four: ant, bee, butterfly, housefly, spider, earthworm, snail, millipede, crab.
3. Vertebrates have a backbone and a skeleton of bones inside; invertebrates have no backbone.
4. Useful: bee or earthworm. Harmful: mosquito, housefly, tick or tapeworm.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Caring for animals and making a portfolio
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: CARING FOR ANIMALS AND MAKING A PORTFOLIO
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Describe ways of caring for animals.
• Make a portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the need to care for animals; b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
A goat tied in the sun all day without water, or a dog that is beaten, suffers just as a person would. Animals feel pain, hunger and thirst, so they depend on people to treat them well.

## Notes
### Why we care for animals
Animals give us food such as milk, eggs, meat and honey. They give us wool and leather, help farmers to plough and carry loads, and keep our homes safe. Cats catch rats, and bees help crops to form fruits. Wild animals attract visitors to Kenya's parks. Animals are living things that can feel pain, so they deserve kindness.

### How to care for animals
- Give them enough clean water and the right food every day.
- Give them a clean, dry shelter that protects them from rain, cold and too much sun.
- Keep their shelter clean by removing dung.
- Take sick animals to a veterinary officer.
- Do not beat, tease, overload or throw stones at animals.
- Do not destroy the nests or homes of birds and other small animals.
- Handle small animals gently and return them to where you found them.

### Staying safe
- Do not touch animals that you do not know, such as stray dogs.
- Keep away from snakes, scorpions, bees and wasps, and tell an adult if you see one.
- Wash your hands with soap and water after touching animals or their droppings.

### Making a portfolio
A portfolio is a collection of your work kept in a file or folder. For this project you will make a portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates:

- Use a file or make a folder from old manila paper or a cereal box.
- Make one section for vertebrates and one for invertebrates.
- Add drawings or pictures cut from old magazines and newspapers.
- Under each picture write the animal's name and one fact, for example: 'Frog – amphibian, has a backbone, lives in water and on land.'
- Keep adding animals you observe during the term.

## Key words
• animal welfare — making sure animals are well fed, healthy and not treated cruelly
• veterinary officer — a person trained to treat sick animals
• portfolio — a collection of a learner's work kept in a file or folder

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A boy sees his neighbour's donkey carrying a very heavy load and being beaten. Is this proper care? What should be done?

Working:
1. Overloading and beating cause the donkey pain.
2. Proper care means a fair load, rest, food and water, and no beating.

Answer: No. The donkey should carry a load it can manage, be given rest, water and food, and never be beaten.

## Activity: Project: portfolio of vertebrates and invertebrates
You will need: Old manila paper, a cereal box or a file, Old magazines and newspapers, Glue, scissors, crayons and pencils
1. In your group, decide on a cover design and the title for your portfolio.
2. Divide the portfolio into two sections: Vertebrates and Invertebrates.
3. Draw or cut out pictures of at least five animals for each section.
4. Write the name of each animal and one fact about it.
5. Share the tasks so that every member contributes, then present your portfolio to the class.

## Practice
1. Give three ways of caring for a pet dog.
2. Why should you wash your hands after handling animals?
3. What is a portfolio?

## Summary
• Animals give us food, materials, help with work and company.
• Care for animals with food, water, shelter, cleanliness and treatment when sick.
• Keep a portfolio to record the vertebrates and invertebrates you study.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: give it food and clean water, give it shelter, keep it clean, take it to a vet when sick, do not beat it.
2. To remove germs from the animal or its droppings that could make you sick.
3. A collection of your work kept in a file or folder.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: How animals feed, grow and breathe
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: HOW ANIMALS FEED, GROW AND BREATHE
============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how feeding, growth and breathing show that animals are living things.
• Give safe examples of each characteristic from animals around you.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the characteristics of animals as living things

## Introduction
A calf drinks milk, then later eats grass, and month by month it becomes a larger cow. Watch its sides while it rests and you will see them move as it breathes.

## Notes
Three characteristics show clearly that animals are living things: they feed, they grow and they breathe. You can observe all three on animals around school and at home, if you watch from a safe distance and do not tease them.

### Feeding
Green plants make their own food. Animals cannot. Every animal must eat.

- Some animals eat plants. Cows, goats, sheep and rabbits eat grass and leaves.
- Some animals eat other animals. A cat hunts rats, a frog eats insects, and an eagle eats small animals.
- Some animals eat both. A hen eats grains and also insects. People eat foods from plants and from animals.

The food becomes the materials an animal uses to grow and to move. A young animal that does not get enough food grows poorly. Do not try to feed wild animals, and do not take food from a farm animal without permission. Observe what they already eat.

### Growth
Growth means the animal gets bigger and its body changes.

- A calf grows into a cow or a bull. Horns may appear as it gets older.
- A chick grows adult feathers and becomes a hen or a cock.
- A tadpole hatches from an egg in water. It has a tail and gills. Later it grows legs, the tail shortens, and it becomes a frog that can live on land.

You can record growth without touching the animal. Compare a young goat with an adult goat: size, horns and coat. If your family keeps chickens, note how a chick looks this month and how it looks next month.

### Breathing
Breathing takes oxygen into the body and pushes used air out.

- Cows, goats, birds, people and adult frogs breathe with lungs. Watch a resting cow: the sides of the body move in and out.
- Fish breathe with gills. Water passes over the gills and oxygen is taken from the water. The covers on the sides of the head open and close. A fish cannot breathe air the way a cow does.
- A tadpole breathes with gills while it lives in water. The adult frog breathes with lungs.

Never hold a fish out of water or cover an animal's nose to test this. Watching is enough evidence that animals breathe.

## Key words
• oxygen — the part of air, and of water, that animals need when they breathe
• lungs — the body parts used for breathing by mammals, birds, reptiles and adult frogs
• tadpole — the young stage of a frog, living in water and breathing with gills

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner lists what a hen does in one morning: it pecks grains, its chest moves as it rests, and the chicks beside it are bigger than they were last month. Which three characteristics are these?

Working:
1. Pecking grains is feeding.
2. The moving chest is breathing.
3. Chicks becoming bigger is growth.

Answer: Feeding, breathing and growth.

### Example 2
Why is it wrong to lift a fish out of a basin for several minutes to "see if it breathes"?

Working:
1. A fish takes oxygen from water using gills.
2. Out of water it cannot breathe properly and can die.

Answer: A fish breathes in water with its gills. Lifting it out can harm or kill it. Watch the gill covers while it is in the water.

## Activity: Record feeding, growth and breathing
You will need: Notebook, A table with columns: Animal, Feeding, Growth, Breathing
1. With your teacher, observe animals around the school compound from a safe distance.
2. For each animal, write what it eats or how it feeds, any sign that it grows, and how it breathes.
3. Use pictures in a book or on a digital device for animals you cannot see, such as a tadpole or a fish.
4. Discuss the table with your group. Add evidence another group found.
5. Do not touch or feed the animals. Wash your hands after the walk.

## Practice
1. Why must animals feed, while green plants do not have to eat?
2. Give one sign of growth in a frog's life.
3. How can you tell that a resting cow is breathing?
4. Name the parts a fish uses to breathe.

## Summary
• Animals feed on plants, other animals, or both.
• Young animals grow and their bodies change as they become adults.
• Mammals, birds and adult frogs use lungs. Fish and tadpoles use gills.

### Answers to practice
1. Animals cannot make their own food. Green plants make food in their leaves.
2. A tadpole grows legs and becomes a frog (or a calf becomes a cow, or a chick grows adult feathers).
3. The sides of its body move in and out.
4. Gills.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Mammals and birds
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: MAMMALS AND BIRDS
===========================

## What you will learn
• Describe the features of mammals and of birds.
• Use those features to sort animals into the two groups.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
A goat has hair and the mother feeds her kid on milk. A dove has feathers and sits on hard-shelled eggs. Both animals have a backbone, but they belong to different groups.

## Notes
Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. They are sorted into five groups. This lesson looks closely at two of those groups: mammals and birds. Both groups have a skeleton of bones inside the body.

### Mammals
Mammals:

- Have a backbone.
- Have hair or fur. A cat's coat is fur. People have hair. Even an elephant has some hairs on its body.
- Feed their young on milk from the mother.
- Include familiar animals that give birth to live young. A cow gives birth to a calf, a goat to a kid, and a dog to puppies.

Mammals you may see near home include cows, goats, sheep, donkeys, dogs, cats and rabbits. Wild mammals include lions, zebras, elephants and monkeys.

Some mammals live in water. A whale and a dolphin have no gills and no scales like a fish. They come to the surface to breathe air, they have a backbone, and the mother feeds the young on milk. They are mammals, not fish.

### Birds
Birds:

- Have a backbone.
- Have feathers, a beak and two wings.
- Have no teeth. The beak matches the food. A hen's beak pecks seeds. A duck's beak is broad for feeding in water.
- Lay eggs with hard shells. A parent keeps the eggs warm until the chicks hatch.

Most birds fly. Feathers and wings make flight possible. An ostrich has feathers and wings but does not fly. It runs on strong legs. A hen flaps for a short distance but does not fly like a dove. Both are still birds because of their feathers and beaks.

### Sorting rule
Look at the body covering and at how the young are fed. Hair or fur, and a baby fed on milk, means a mammal. Feathers and a beak mean a bird. If you are building a portfolio, put these animals on the vertebrates pages and write the group name under each picture.

## Key words
• fur — the hairy coat of many mammals
• beak — the hard mouth of a bird, used for feeding
• milk — the food a mammal mother produces for her young

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these animals into mammals and birds: cat, ostrich, dolphin, dove, goat.

Working:
1. Cat, dolphin and goat have a backbone, and the young are fed on milk. They are mammals.
2. Ostrich and dove have feathers and beaks. They are birds.

Answer: Mammals: cat, dolphin, goat. Birds: ostrich, dove.

### Example 2
An ostrich cannot fly. A classmate says it is therefore not a bird. What features show that it is a bird?

Working:
1. Birds are identified by feathers, a beak, wings and hard-shelled eggs.
2. Flight is common but not the feature that decides the group.

Answer: An ostrich has feathers, wings and a beak, and it lays hard-shelled eggs. Those features make it a bird.

## Activity: Picture sort: mammal or bird
You will need: Pictures from old magazines, newspapers or a digital search the teacher guides, Two large sheets labelled Mammals and Birds, Glue or a notebook for drawing
1. Collect or draw at least four mammals and four birds. Search print or digital materials for any animal you are not sure about.
2. Place each picture on the correct sheet and write one feature that proves your choice, such as "fur" or "feathers".
3. Include one tricky animal, such as a dolphin or an ostrich, and explain it to the class.
4. Add the best pictures to the vertebrates section of your portfolio.
5. Take care of the books and devices you use, and return them neatly.

## Practice
1. State two features of a mammal.
2. Why is a dolphin a mammal and not a fish?
3. State two features of a bird.
4. A hen does not fly long distances. Is it still a bird? Why?

## Summary
• Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.
• Birds have feathers and a beak, and they lay hard-shelled eggs.
• Whales and dolphins are mammals. An ostrich is a bird even though it does not fly.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: has a backbone, has hair or fur, feeds young on milk, gives birth to live young (for familiar mammals).
2. It breathes air, has a backbone, and feeds its young on milk. It does not have gills.
3. Any two: feathers, beak, wings, hard-shelled eggs, a backbone.
4. Yes. It has feathers, wings and a beak, and it lays hard-shelled eggs.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Reptiles, amphibians and fish
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: REPTILES, AMPHIBIANS AND FISH
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the features of reptiles, amphibians and fish.
• Sort vertebrates into these three groups using skin, breathing and where they live.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment

## Introduction
A lizard basks on a warm wall, a frog sits at the edge of a puddle, and a tilapia stays under the water. All three have a backbone, yet each belongs to a different group.

## Notes
The other three groups of vertebrates are reptiles, amphibians and fish. Each group has a backbone. The skin, the place they live and the way they breathe help you tell them apart.

### Reptiles
Reptiles have dry skin covered with scales. Most of them lay eggs on land. The shell of the egg is leathery, not hard like a bird's egg.

- A lizard has four legs and a tail, and it often rests in the sun.
- A snake has no legs, but it has a long backbone and scaly skin, so it is a reptile.
- A crocodile lives near water, but it has scaly skin and breathes with lungs.
- A tortoise has a shell on the outside and a backbone inside. That backbone makes it a vertebrate. A snail also has a shell, but a snail has no backbone, so a snail is an invertebrate.

Do not pick up snakes or go near crocodiles. Observe them only from far away, or use pictures in a book.

### Amphibians
Amphibians have soft, moist skin and no scales. They use both water and land. Frogs and toads lay eggs in water. The eggs have no hard shell. A frog's egg hatches into a tadpole, which breathes with gills. The tadpole grows legs and becomes an adult frog that breathes with lungs and can hop on land. A toad is also an amphibian. Its skin is bumpier than a frog's, but it still needs moisture and still begins life in water.

### Fish
Fish live in water. They have fins, and most have scales. They breathe with gills, not lungs. Tilapia and catfish are fish. Most fish lay eggs in water. When a fish is prepared as food you can see the backbone running along the body. That backbone is the evidence that a fish is a vertebrate.

### A quick test
Ask three questions. Is the skin dry and scaly? Think of a reptile. Is the skin moist, and does the animal use both water and land? Think of an amphibian. Does it have fins and gills and live in water? Think of a fish. Then remember that all three groups have a backbone, so all of them are vertebrates.

## Key words
• scales — the small hard plates that cover the skin of reptiles and most fish
• reptile — a vertebrate with dry scaly skin, such as a lizard, snake, crocodile or tortoise
• fins — the flat parts a fish uses for swimming

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these vertebrates: toad, catfish, snake, tortoise.

Working:
1. A toad has moist skin and uses water and land: amphibian.
2. A catfish has fins and gills: fish.
3. A snake and a tortoise have dry scaly skin: reptiles.

Answer: Toad: amphibian. Catfish: fish. Snake and tortoise: reptiles.

### Example 2
A tortoise and a snail both have shells. Which one is a vertebrate, and why?

Working:
1. A vertebrate must have a backbone inside the body.
2. A tortoise has a backbone. A snail does not.

Answer: The tortoise is a vertebrate because it has a backbone. The snail is an invertebrate.

## Activity: Three-group chart
You will need: Manila paper or an exercise book, Pictures or a textbook, Coloured pencils
1. Divide a page into three columns: Reptiles, Amphibians, Fish.
2. Search print or digital materials and write two examples in each column, plus one feature of that group.
3. Add a note on how each group breathes: lungs or gills.
4. Share the chart with another group and correct any animal placed in the wrong column.
5. Do not bring live snakes, frogs from protected places, or fish out of water into class. Use pictures.

## Practice
1. Why is a snake a reptile even though it has no legs?
2. Where do frogs lay their eggs, and what hatches from them?
3. State two features of a fish.
4. Name the five groups of vertebrates.

## Summary
• Reptiles have dry scaly skin. Most lay eggs on land.
• Amphibians have moist skin and begin life in water, like a frog and its tadpole.
• Fish have fins and gills and live in water. All three groups are vertebrates.

### Answers to practice
1. It has a backbone and dry scaly skin, and it is not a fish, amphibian, bird or mammal.
2. In water. A tadpole hatches from the egg.
3. Any two: lives in water, has fins, has scales, breathes with gills, has a backbone.
4. Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Insects and other invertebrates
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: INSECTS AND OTHER INVERTEBRATES
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Identify an insect using its body parts and six legs.
• Give examples of useful and harmful invertebrates and handle them safely.

Curriculum outcomes: b) distinguish vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment; c) appreciate the need to care for animals

## Introduction
Count the legs on a grasshopper and you will find six. Count the legs on a spider and you will find eight. That count, together with the missing backbone, tells you how to sort these small animals.

## Notes
Most of the animals on Earth have no backbone. They are invertebrates. Many are small, and you can find them in the school compound if you look carefully under leaves, stones and near flowers. Look without hurting them.

### Insects
An insect is an invertebrate with:

- A body in three parts, called the head, the thorax and the abdomen.
- Six legs, all joined to the thorax.
- A pair of feelers on the head.
- Often wings on the adult. Butterflies, bees and houseflies have wings. The ants you see walking on a path usually have no wings, but they still have six legs and three body parts, so they are insects.

Count the legs before you decide. A spider has eight legs, so a spider is not an insect. A millipede has many more than six legs. An earthworm has no legs at all. All of these are still invertebrates, because none of them has a backbone.

### Other invertebrates nearby
Earthworms live in moist soil. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil, and their waste adds useful matter to the soil. Snails have a soft body and a shell. The shell is not a backbone. Millipedes curl up when touched. That response shows they are living things, and the lack of a backbone shows they are invertebrates.

### Useful and harmful invertebrates
Some invertebrates help people. Bees visit flowers, help fruits to form, and make honey. Earthworms improve soil for crops. Some invertebrates cause harm. Mosquitoes can spread malaria. Houseflies land on dirt and then on uncovered food, carrying germs. Ticks bite livestock and can spread disease to the animals. Some worms can live inside the human intestine and make a person ill. That is one reason people take deworming medicine when a health worker or a parent gives it.

### Safety and care
Use a stick or a leaf to turn a stone, not your bare hands. Do not touch bees, wasps, spiders, scorpions or centipedes. Do not destroy nests or pull wings off insects. If you put a small animal in a jar to look at it, make holes in the lid, look for a short time, and put the animal back where you found it. Wash your hands afterwards. Caring for animals includes these small ones. Add your drawings to the invertebrates section of your portfolio.

## Key words
• thorax — the middle body part of an insect, where the legs and wings are joined
• abdomen — the rear body part of an insect
• feelers — the pair of long parts on an insect's head, used for sensing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner finds a small animal with eight legs and no wings. A second animal has six legs, three body parts and wings. Which one is an insect?

Working:
1. Insects have six legs and three body parts.
2. Eight legs means the first animal is not an insect. It is likely a spider.

Answer: The animal with six legs, three body parts and wings is an insect. The eight-legged animal is not.

### Example 2
Name one helpful invertebrate and one harmful invertebrate, and state what each does.

Working:
1. Bees help flowers form fruits and make honey. Earthworms improve soil.
2. Mosquitoes can spread malaria. Houseflies carry germs to food. Ticks harm livestock.

Answer: Helpful: a bee, which helps fruits to form, or an earthworm, which improves soil. Harmful: a mosquito, a housefly or a tick.

## Activity: Invertebrate hunt with a safety rule
You will need: Notebook, A hand lens if available, A clear jar with holes in the lid, Portfolio folder
1. Walk in the school compound with your teacher and look for invertebrates on plants, in soil and near flowers.
2. Record each animal, the number of legs if you can see them, and whether you think it is an insect.
3. Do not touch bees, wasps, spiders, scorpions, centipedes or snakes. Put any animal you jar back in the same place.
4. Mark one helpful and one harmful invertebrate on your list and explain each to your group.
5. Wash your hands, then file the list in your portfolio under Invertebrates.

## Practice
1. State two features that show an animal is an insect.
2. Why is a spider not an insect?
3. Give one way earthworms help plants.
4. What should you do after observing small animals?

## Summary
• Insects have six legs and three body parts, and they have no backbone.
• Spiders, worms, snails and millipedes are invertebrates but not all of them are insects.
• Observe small animals gently, learn which ones help or harm, and wash your hands.

### Answers to practice
1. Six legs and a body in three parts (also feelers, and often wings). It has no backbone.
2. A spider has eight legs. An insect has six.
3. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil, and their waste makes the soil richer.
4. Return them to the place you found them and wash your hands.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of animals as living things?
options: They make their own food from sunlight
questions.explanation: Animals eat ready-made food. Green plants make their own food.

questions.question: A goat runs away when a dog barks at it. This shows that animals:
questions.explanation: Running away from danger is a response to a change in the environment.

questions.question: Name two ways in which animals remove waste.
questions.answer: Passing out urine and droppings (also sweating and breathing out used air).
questions.explanation: Removing waste keeps harmful substances out of the body.

questions.question: Fish breathe using:
questions.explanation: Gills take in oxygen from the water.

questions.question: An animal with a backbone is called:
questions.explanation: Vertebrates are animals that have a backbone.

questions.question: Which of these animals is an invertebrate?
Which group of animals are ALL vertebrates?
questions.explanation: Cow (mammal), snake (reptile) and dove (bird) all have backbones.

questions.question: A crab has a hard outer covering. Is it a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: A hard outer covering is not a backbone. A crab has no backbone.

questions.question: Which of these is a proper way of caring for animals?
options: Tying a goat in the sun all day
Giving clean water and a dry shelter
questions.explanation: Animals need water, food and shelter to stay healthy.

questions.question: Give one reason why we should care for animals.
questions.answer: Any one: they give us food such as milk, eggs and meat; they help us with work; they can feel pain; they give us materials such as leather and wool.
questions.explanation: People depend on animals, and animals can suffer when mistreated.

questions.question: Which group has feathers and a beak?
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers, a beak and wings, and they lay hard-shelled eggs.

questions.question: An animal has six legs and three body parts. It is:
questions.explanation: Insects are invertebrates with six legs and a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
